## Appendix F HSE and safety

This appendix gives the public incident history for mooring lines and station keeping, the recorded failure modes and causes, and the lessons that apply to this design.

### F.1 Data used

| Source | Records read | Records for this equipment | Period | Read on | Ref. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BSEE Incident Investigations raw data | 2032 | 7 | 1995-01-04 to 2026-10-24 | 2026-11-12 | [H1] |

The records are matched to the equipment by rules on the source's own fields. A cause is listed only where the source states it.

### F.2 Incident history

The data holds 7 records whose event type names this equipment, dated 2004-08-26 to 2025-03-28 [H1]. Records with a fatality: 0; with an injury: 0; with pollution: 4.
The count is a lower bound: 2 of the 3 cases in Section F.4 are not among these records, because the event type recorded for them does not name this equipment or the data set does not hold them.
Includes loss-of-station events of dynamically positioned units, which the source event type does not separate from moored units.

### F.3 Failure modes and stated causes

A record with two event types counts under both, so the counts can add up to more than the number of records.

| Failure mode | Records |

| Loss of station or mooring failure | 6 |
| Loss of containment (leak, release, spill) | 4 |
| Unplanned or emergency disconnect | 2 |

None of the 7 records states a cause: the data set gives the event type only. The causes on record are those in the investigation reports of Section F.4.

### F.4 Illustrative public cases

**Case 1: Tension-leg platform, Green Canyon block 237, US Gulf of Mexico, 2005-09-23** [H2]

- What failed: The tendon bottom connector system. Three recovered bottom connectors had separated bodies and their lock rings were missing (p. 3);
- Failure mode: Loss of station or mooring failure; Structural damage or collapse;
- Cause stated by the investigation: The most probable cause of the capsize was loss of integrity of the mooring system on one pontoon, specifically the bottom connector system at two piles (p. 4);
- Cause stated by the investigation: Metallurgical analysis of recovered material, believed to be from the load shoulder, showed evidence of shear ductile overload and plastic deformation (p. 4);
- Cause stated by the investigation: Maximum conditions in the hurricane were below the 1000-year storm criteria, and there was no evidence of direct collision (p. 4);
- Mechanism as stated: Overload;
- Consequence: The facility capsized and was a complete loss (p. 5);

**Case 2: Spar, Alaminos Canyon block 25, US Gulf of Mexico, 2021-07-18** [H3]

- What failed: One of 12 mooring lines was lost when a 160 mm grade R4 chain link failed after about 20 years in service; the link had two fractures, one at a crown and one at the flash weld (p. 2);
- Failure mode: Loss of station or mooring failure;
- Cause stated by the investigation: The fractures initiated from hydrogen embrittlement. The link's material properties were not satisfactory for grade R4 chain; its high hardness made it susceptible and was likely the result of improper heat treatment (p. 3);
- Cause stated by the investigation: There was no evidence that stress from out-of-plane bending or twisting contributed to the fractures (p. 2);
- Mechanism as stated: Hydrogen embrittlement;
- Consequence: No injury or pollution was recorded; the cost was estimated at 10 million US dollars (p. 3);

**Case 3: Spar, Mississippi Canyon block 941, US Gulf of Mexico, 2023-06-19** [H4]

- What failed: A 5-inch grade RQ4 chain link in one of 12 mooring lines parted in service (p. 2);
- Failure mode: Loss of station or mooring failure;
- Cause stated by the investigation: The line most likely failed due to fatigue that initiated at the top of the link crown, where stresses are high (p. 3);
- Cause stated by the investigation: Corrosion likely contributed to the crown cracks, but the corrosion mechanism could not be determined; hydrogen may have contributed, but the fracture surfaces were too corroded to confirm it (p. 3);
- Cause stated by the investigation: Contributing cause, a weakness in the maintenance management programme for the mooring system, where reliance on third-party vendors delayed corrective maintenance (p. 3);
- Mechanism as stated: Fatigue;
- Consequence: Replacement of the line was estimated at 5 million US dollars (p. 4);

### F.5 Lessons for this design

| Finding or recommendation stated by the investigation | Case | Addressed in |
|---|---|---|
| The regulator recommended a study of this mooring system, to find possible quick fixes for existing tension-leg platforms that use it and to decide whether it remains acceptable for floating installations (p. 5) | 1 | Section 4.3: this system is a chain and polyester spread mooring with no tendon bottom connector; the connector capacities are checked in Section 6.2 |
| Follow-up hardness testing of links up to 15 links away from the failure found high hardness in each tested link (p. 3) | 2 | Section 4.4: chain grade and maximum hardness are stated in the material data; Section 3.3 recommends hardness records for every chain batch |
| The report records that a significant decrease in the tension of this line was found on a daily marine report on 11 March 2022 (p. 3) | 3 | Section 6.3: top-chain fatigue life; Section 3.3 recommends a line-tension alarm with a stated response time |
